history.nameOrigin: After the nuclear physicist Yuri Oganessian, a leader of superheavy-element research; the second element named after a living person.
history.symbolNote: Temporary name: ununoctium (Uuo); named oganesson in 2016.
history.note: Made from calcium-48 on californium-249; the 2016 IUPAC/IUPAP report credited the Dubna–Livermore collaboration. A 1999 Berkeley claim was retracted.

prose.text: Oganesson is the heaviest element known, a synthetic member of group 18 below radon, named after the nuclear physicist Yuri Oganessian, who was alive when it was named; only seaborgium shares that distinction. Its discovery was announced in October 2006 by the Dubna laboratory and Lawrence Livermore: a long bombardment of californium-249 with calcium-48 ions had yielded just three atoms of oganesson-294, an isotope with a half-life of about half a millisecond. No chemistry has been possible. Its predicted configuration fills the 7p shell, [Rn] 5f¹⁴ 6d¹⁰ 7s² 7p⁶, yet calculations suggest relativity blurs its shell structure and that it might even be a solid, not a gas, at room temperature.
